summary: For ages 8-9: order and compare numbers beyond 1000 using >, <, = by scanning from the highest place value down (thousands, then hundreds, tens, ones), descending to the next place only when a place ties. This generalises the three-digit most-significant-digit-first procedure to four digits and beyond, in line with the Year 4 objective to 'order and compare numbers beyond 1000'. Core moves: right-align numbers by place, compare the highest place first, and justify each decision by place value. Stress-test with same-leading-digit pairs (4,562 vs 4,526), mixed-length pairs (987 vs 1,024), and multi-zero numbers (4,050 vs 4,005). Progress from single comparisons to ordering whole sets using real contexts such as populations and distances.
misconceptions: Comparing by number of digits incorrectly, or by the largest single digit.
Not descending to the next place on a tie (declaring equal too early).
Aligning numbers to the left instead of by place value (mixed lengths).
Reversing the symbol or binding it to reading order.

activities.title: Place-aligned comparison bench
steps: Take two numbers (including different lengths like 987 and 1,024) and write or place them so the digits stack by place value, right-justified into a place-value chart.
Starting at the highest place, compare column by column; mark each tied place and move down one place only when the current place is equal.
Place a > or < symbol between the numbers based on the first place that differs, and say which place decided it; use = only if every place ties.
Work the trap pairs: 4,562 vs 4,526 (same thousands and hundreds), 4,050 vs 4,005 (multi-zero), and 987 vs 1,024 (mixed length).
Then order a set of 5 numbers from smallest to largest using real data such as city populations, justifying each neighbouring comparison by place value.
activities.insight: Once two numbers are lined up by place, the larger number is decided at the first (highest) place where they differ, not by which number has a big digit somewhere. On a tie you keep going down to the next place; if every place ties, the numbers are equal. For whole numbers written without leading zeros, the number with more digits is always larger, because it reaches a higher place.

activities.title: Number-line placement for magnitude
steps: Place given numbers (e.g. 8,091; 8,901; 8,910) at their approximate positions on a 0–10,000 number line.
Use the positions to read off the order from smallest to largest.
Check the line ordering against the place-value scan and resolve any disagreement by column comparison.
activities.insight: Ordering reflects magnitude on the number line, and the place-value scan should agree with where numbers sit on the line.

activities.title: Convince-me: rebut the big-digit claim
steps: Read a character's claim such as '987 > 1,024 because it has more big digits'.
Write or say a rebuttal that aligns the numbers by place and names the deciding place.
Give a second example (e.g. 999 vs 1,001) that shows why a big single digit does not make a number larger.
activities.insight: Justifying a comparison out loud forces the most-significant-place reasoning to the surface and exposes big-digit and left-alignment shortcuts as faulty.

activities.title: Annotated worked scan (reference)
steps: Step through a worked comparison where thousands are equal, then hundreds decide, noting at each step whether the place ties or decides.
Use this as a reference model before attempting fresh pairs independently.
activities.insight: The procedure is: compare highest place first, descend only on a tie, stop at the first differing place.

checkQuestion: Watch them compare and order beyond 1000. 'Put a symbol between 3,472 and 3,427. Now order these: 8,910; 8,091; 8,901. Tell me which place you looked at and why.' The 3,472/3,427 pair (same digits) forces highest-place-first reasoning.
checkAnswer: 3,472 > 3,427; order 8,091 < 8,901 < 8,910; comparing from the highest place value down.
